report.headline: workerd pairs strong core engineering (a deep, hierarchical AGENTS.md network, an exceptionally rigorous test suite, and a mature CI/release pipeline) with AI adoption that is still nascent in practice and supply-chain security hardening that lags well behind the trust this runtime demands.

An exceptionally deep test suite (884 files, 1.86 test-to-source ratio) spanning unit, Cap'n-Proto integration, Web Platform Tests, and sanitizer builds.

Comprehensive documentation (deep README, /docs, CONTRIBUTING, CODEOWNERS) that doubles as agent-readable context.
risks: Supply-chain security-as-code is thin for a repo this sensitive: a flagged dangerous-workflow pattern, almost no pinned Action references (2/63), no signed releases, and no SBOM.

Default branch protection sets required approvals to 0 and doesn't mandate PRs, so the review discipline seen in practice (0.7 avg reviews/PR) isn't backstopped by a hard gate.
No committed dependency-update automation, leaving dependency freshness/security patching to manual or undocumented processes.
No evals/golden-test harness for the LLM step already running in CI, so that AI-assisted automation lacks a measurable regression check.

report.headline: Cloudflare workers-sdk pairs a genuinely mature guardrail foundation — a huge, behaviorally meaningful test suite and a 31-workflow CI/CD pipeline — with only nascent, mostly mechanical AI-workflow integration, placing the org solidly in L3 Augmented with a few L4 Integrated signals (LLM-in-CI, dependency automation) still thin on systemic review loops and release-integrity hardening.
strengths: Exceptional automated test suite (1210 files, 0.51 test-to-source ratio, e2e + API-schema validation) that makes AI-generated changes safe to verify before merge
Mature, multi-stage CI/CD with 31 workflows, changesets-driven automated releases, and broad dependency automation across ecosystems
Layered AI agent guidance — root AGENTS.md plus per-package AGENTS.md (create-cloudflare, miniflare) — giving agents concrete, package-specific build/test/architecture context
Enforced code-quality gates (a composite pnpm check spanning lint/type/format/pinned-deps) plus CODEOWNERS-driven review
Strong supply-chain hygiene in specific areas: SAST on every PR/push, 100% Action pinning by SHA, and a published SECURITY.md
risks: Multiple CI workflows accept untrusted input into privileged pull_request_target contexts — a concrete injection/secret-exfiltration risk that would undermine trust in any more autonomous CI activity
Releases of a widely-installed CLI ship with no artifact signing/provenance and no SBOM, leaving no cryptographic way to verify what actually shipped
AI involvement in the PR/review loop is still marginal (~3%) with no dedicated AI review bot — visible automation is mechanical (bots, dependency bumps) rather than agentic
Branch-protection ruleset requires 0 approvals and no status checks, so today's strong review discipline rests on convention rather than a system guarantee
Miniflare has temporarily disabled several shared lint rules, a tracked but still-open guardrail gap in one of the core packages

roadmap.title: A handful of CI workflows accept untrusted input into privileged contexts
roadmap.rationale: pull_request_target workflows run with access to secrets/write tokens while checking out untrusted fork code; if a PR title, branch name, or comment body is templated into a run: step, that's a classic path to secret exfiltration or unauthorized write access — worth resolving before leaning on CI for more autonomous, agent-driven actions.
explore: Has anyone walked through what a fork PR with a crafted title or branch name could do inside bonk.yml or the codeowners.yml workflow?
Is there appetite to split untrusted-input handling from the privileged pull_request_target context, e.g. via a two-workflow hand-off pattern?

roadmap.title: AI shows up in commits and CI, but doesn't yet close the loop on review or verification
roadmap.rationale: Right now AI touches roughly 3% of PRs and the rest of the automation (Dependabot, changesets bots) is mechanical rather than agentic; extending trust to agents on more of the day-to-day workflow usually needs a visible harness — evals/golden tests plus an AI review step — so the team isn't relying on standard human review alone to catch AI mistakes.
explore: If more day-to-day changes were agent-drafted, what evidence would make the team comfortable merging them at the current pace?
Would a lightweight eval harness for AI-touched changes, or an AI-review bot, change how much autonomy feels safe to extend?

roadmap.title: Releases ship without signed provenance or an SBOM
roadmap.rationale: wrangler has a large install footprint; without artifact signing (cosign/SLSA) or an SBOM, downstream consumers — and any future automated release agent — have no cryptographic way to confirm what actually shipped, which becomes more important as more of the release path is automated.
explore: Given wrangler's install base, would provenance attestation change how confidently the release pipeline could be left to run unattended?
Has an SBOM ever come up in a downstream security questionnaire or customer ask?

roadmap.title: Agent guidance lives mostly in AGENTS.md while the top-level CLAUDE.md carries no content of its own
roadmap.rationale: Delegating CLAUDE.md to AGENTS.md is reasonable, but as more agent tools adopt their own convention-file expectations, it's worth checking whether today's guidance actually answers the questions agents get stuck on — especially explicit constraints (pnpm-only, workerd/version-lockstep rules) that aren't spelled out as hard 'never' statements.
explore: When an agent has gone off-track in this repo, was it because AGENTS.md didn't cover the situation, or because the guidance existed but wasn't followed?
Are there a handful of 'never do X' rules (e.g. around pnpm vs npm, or workerd version bumps) that keep coming up informally and might be worth stating explicitly?

roadmap.title: Review discipline looks strong in practice, but isn't yet backed by a hard branch-protection requirement
roadmap.rationale: The sampled merged PRs show 100% review coverage and an average of 3.2 reviewers, but the branch-protection ruleset itself requires 0 approvals and no status checks — that's a cultural norm today, not a system guarantee, which matters more as PR volume or agent-driven contributions grow.
explore: Is the team's confidence that 'PRs always get reviewed' resilient to a busier period or a new contributor unfamiliar with the norms?
Would codifying a required-approval rule change anything day to day, or mostly just formalize what already happens?

discrepancies.claim: D1's signalScore of 50 may undercount depth: the sampled evidence shows not just root CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md but distinct, content-rich per-package AGENTS.md files (create-cloudflare, miniflare) documenting concrete build/lint/test conventions, which is more than a typical single-file stub.

D8's signalScore of 31 may not credit the multiple nested AGENTS.md files (root, create-cloudflare, miniflare) as a distributed agent-spec library analogous to the 'agents/ with multiple specs' criterion it looks for.
